Where it began

Michael Atherton was born in Failsworth, Lancashire, on 23 March 1968. At Manchester Grammar School he captained the first eleven and scored close to 3,500 runs. He was soon leading England's under-19 side, at just 16.

He read history at Downing College, Cambridge, and won a Blue there. His county debut for Lancashire brought 73, and a fortnight later came his maiden first-class century. In 1989 he took the Combined Universities, as captain, all the way to the last eight of the Benson & Hedges Cup.

The player

He first played for England in 1989, against Australia at Trent Bridge. His real arrival came in 1990: in his first Test as an opener he made 151 against New Zealand, and he put on 204 with Graham Gooch against India at Lord's. That summer he was named Young Cricketer of the Year.

In all he played 115 Tests up to 2001 and made 7,728 runs at 37.70, with 16 hundreds and 46 fifties. He was made captain in 1993, aged 25, and led England in 55 Tests. Two late highlights were match-winning hundreds in 2000, at the Oval against the West Indies and in Karachi, which brought England rare series wins over both.

What made him special

He was at his best when things were at their worst. His 185 not out against South Africa lasted 643 minutes and saved a Test that seemed lost. His duels with Allan Donald became part of cricket folklore. Steve Waugh nicknamed him the Cockroach, as a tribute to how hard he was to get rid of.

Australia, it must be said, were not his favourite opponents. Glenn McGrath in particular seemed to have his number. But England's batting in the 1990s was often fragile, and he was the man asked to hold it together.

Away from the middle

After he stopped playing, he found a second career that might even outshine the first. He wrote for The Sunday Telegraph, became cricket correspondent of The Times in 2008, and commentated for Channel 4 and then Sky Sports from 2005. The British Press Awards named him their Sports Journalist of the Year in 2010, and the Sports Journalists' Association made him its Sports Writer of the Year in 2009 and 2011. He also wrote an autobiography, Opening Up. He is an OBE and a Wisden Cricketer of the Year.

His son Josh de Caires followed him into the game, making his first-class debut for Middlesex in 2021.

And finally

Viewers came to know him for his dry, unfussy humour on air. His first England cap reached him when David Gower, the captain, threw a plastic bag of kit at him. It was an informal start for a man who would go on to lead the side more times than most.
